lesson_title: Taste the Soup, But Stir It First
hook_text: You do not drink the whole pot to check the salt. You taste a spoonful. Statistics works the same way, with one rule people forget.
clip_script: Want to know how 1200 learners get to school? You do not have to ask all 1200. The whole school is the pot, the population. The 60 you actually ask are the spoonful, the sample. But here is the rule: stir first. If the salt has sunk and you taste the top, you get the wrong answer. Ask only the Grade 12s, or only whoever is standing near you, and your spoonful is unstirred: the answer leans their way. That is a biased sample. Three ways to stir. Random: names from a hat. Systematic: every 20th name on the register, 1200 gives 60. Stratified: 15 from each of four grades, so nobody is left out. Then scale up with care: 42 of 60 walk to school, that is 70 percent, so about 840 of the 1200 probably walk. About. A spoonful is an estimate, not a census. Say it: taste the soup, but stir it first.
visual_style: A soup pot on a whiteboard with a ladle lifting a spoonful; salt grains sink to the bottom and the top spoon comes up empty; a register scrolls with every 20th name glowing; four grade blocks each give up 15 dots; 42 of 60 dots scale to about 840.
pacing: Pot and spoon fast, the unstirred spoon with a beat, three stirring methods in a rhythm, the scale-up at speaking pace.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for posing countable questions, questionnaire design and choosing a data source.
